question: Write describeType(value) that returns null for null, array for arrays, date for Date objects, object for other objects and the typeof string for everything else. Print the result for 1, 'a', null, [1], new Date(0) and { a: 1 }.
Print the typeof of seven values: the string hi, the number 42, true, undefined, Symbol('id'), 10n and null, joined by a pipe. Predict which one will surprise you.
answer:
typeof reports the tag the engine stored, and null shares the object tag, so it is the last entry that comes out wrong.

code:
const types = ['hi', 42, true, undefined, Symbol('id'), 10n, null];
const tags = types.map((value) => typeof value);
console.log(tags.join(' | ')); // string | number | boolean | undefined | symbol | bigint | object
console.log(new Set(tags).size + ' distinct tags from ' + types.length + ' values'); // 7 distinct tags from 7 values

output:
string | number | boolean | undefined | symbol | bigint | object
7 distinct tags from 7 values

question: Write isPrimitive(value) that returns true for strings, numbers, booleans, null and undefined but false for objects, arrays and functions. Run it over [1, 'a', true, null, undefined, {}, () => 1] and print the results.

Show three ways to recognise the array [1, 2] as an array: typeof, Array.isArray and instanceof. Print them, then print Array.isArray for the string 'abc' and for the array-like object { length: 2, 0: 1, 1: 2 }.
answer:
typeof only says object, so you need Array.isArray for a real check. instanceof works too but fails across separate copies of the code.

code:
const value = [1, 2];
const lookalike = { length: 2, 0: 1, 1: 2 };
console.log(typeof value, Array.isArray(value), value instanceof Array); // object true true
console.log(Array.isArray('abc'), Array.isArray(lookalike)); // false false

output:
object true true
false false

question: Turn the string 'abc' into a number, print the value and its typeof, then print Number.isNaN of it and the global isNaN of it. Also print isNaN('12'). Expected: NaN, number, true, true, then false.
answer:
NaN has the number tag, so typeof cannot spot it. Number.isNaN only accepts real numbers while the global isNaN converts its argument first.

code:
const bad = Number('abc');
console.log(typeof bad, bad); // number NaN
console.log(Number.isNaN(bad), isNaN(bad)); // true true
console.log(isNaN('12')); // false

output:
number NaN
true true
false

question: Print the typeof of a declared but unassigned let variable and of a name that was never declared at all. Expected: undefined for both, with no ReferenceError.
answer:
typeof is the only operator that is allowed to look at a name that does not exist, which makes it safe for feature checks.

code:
let declared;
console.log(typeof declared); // undefined
console.log(typeof neverDeclared); // undefined, no ReferenceError
console.log(typeof declared + '|' + typeof neverDeclared); // undefined|undefined

output:
undefined
undefined
undefined|undefined

question: Print Object.prototype.toString.call for null, an empty array and a Date, then print typeof for the same three values to show where the two disagree.
answer:
The internal tag survives null and arrays, so the toString call gives a sharper label than typeof when you need to log what really came back.

code:
const values = [null, [], new Date(0)];
const internal = values.map((value) => Object.prototype.toString.call(value));
console.log(internal.join(' ')); // [object Null] [object Array] [object Date]
console.log(values.map((value) => typeof value).join(' ')); // object object object

output:
[object Null] [object Array] [object Date]
object object object

question: Compare the primitive string 'chrome' with new String('chrome'). Print both typeof values, then print whether they are loosely equal, strictly equal and equal after unboxing with valueOf.
answer:
The boxed version is a real object, so strict equality fails while valueOf hands back the primitive text underneath.

code:
const primitive = 'chrome';
const boxed = new String('chrome');
console.log(typeof primitive, typeof boxed); // string object
console.log(boxed == primitive, boxed === primitive, boxed.valueOf() === primitive); // true false true

output:
string object
true false true

question: Declare a normal function, an arrow function and a class, print the typeof of all three, then print whether each one has a prototype property.
Create the regular expression /abc/, a Map with one entry and a Set with two entries. Print their typeof values and their instanceof results.
Create a symbol with the label token, then print its typeof and its toString result, the typeof of its description, and whether it equals a second Symbol('token') you make.
answer:
A symbol is a primitive with a unique hidden identity. Two symbols with the same label are still different values, which is what makes them safe as map keys.

code:
const token = Symbol('token');
console.log(typeof token, token.toString()); // symbol Symbol(token)
console.log(token.description, typeof token.description); // token string
console.log(token === Symbol('token')); // false

output:
symbol Symbol(token)
token string
false

question: Print the typeof of the bigint literal 9007199254740993n and of the number 42, then add 1n to the bigint and print the result next to Number.isInteger of it.
answer:
Bigint and number look alike in code but carry different tags, which is why mixing them in one arithmetic expression is a mistake.

code:
const big = 9007199254740993n;
const small = 42;
console.log(typeof big, typeof small); // bigint number
console.log(big + 1n, Number.isInteger(Number(big))); // 9007199254740994n true

output:
bigint number
9007199254740994n true

question: Create a TypeError with the message boom and a plain Error with the same message. Print the TypeError typeof, whether it is an instance of Error, its name, its message and whether the two errors are equal.
answer:
Errors are objects with extra fields, so typeof calls them plain objects and you need instanceof to recognise one. Each new error is a separate object.

code:
const failure = new TypeError('boom');
const plain = new Error('boom');
console.log(typeof failure, failure instanceof Error); // object true
console.log(failure.name, failure.message); // TypeError boom
console.log(failure === plain); // false

output:
object true
TypeError boom
false

question: Write countTypes(values) that returns an object counting how many values of each typeof the array holds. Run it on [1, 'a', true, 2, 'b'] and print the JSON.
Write firstTypeMismatch(a, b) that returns the index where the two arrays first hold values of different typeof, or -1 when they agree. Test [1,2,3] against [1,'2',3] and [1] against [1,'x'].
Write describeList(values) that maps every value to the text value:typeof, and print the result for [1, '1', null] joined by spaces.

Write typeSummary(values) that reports how many values there are, how many distinct typeof tags they use and the tags in alphabetical order. Example: [1, 'a', 2, true] gives 4 values, 3 types: boolean,number,string.
Write groupByType(values) that returns an object whose keys are the typeof tags and whose values are arrays of the string versions of the matching values. Run it on [1, 'a', 2] and print the JSON.
Print the typeof of 0 / 0 and of Infinity, then print whether Infinity is bigger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and whether Number.isNaN and Number.isFinite approve of the two values.
answer:
Both of these odd numbers are still numbers as far as the type tag is concerned, which is why typeof alone cannot guard your arithmetic.

code:
const notANumber = 0 / 0;
const tooBig = Infinity;
console.log(typeof notANumber, notANumber); // number NaN
console.log(typeof tooBig, tooBig > Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER); // number true
console.log(Number.isNaN(notANumber), Number.isFinite(tooBig)); // true false

output:
number NaN
number true
true false

question: Write isFiniteNumber(value) that is true only for real finite numbers, and run it over [1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity, '2']. Expected: true, true, false, false, false.
Write describeSize(value) that returns bigint:10 for the bigint 10n and number:true for the number 10, so a caller can tell the two apart. Print both results.
Write typeMap(obj) that turns the keys and values of an object into key:typeof strings joined by commas. Run it on { id: 7, name: 'cart', items: [], paid: false, note: null }.

Take the response { data: { id: 1 } } and print the typeof of a missing items field and of a missing error field. Then read one level deeper and catch the error that reading a field of undefined throws.
Write display(value) that returns MISSING for undefined, NULL for null and tag:value for everything else, then print the results for [undefined, null, 'undefined', 0].
Write isEmptyValue(value) that returns true for null, undefined, a blank string and an empty array but false for the number 0. Print the results for '', ' ', 0, [], null and 'x'.
Write countObjects(values) that counts only the values whose typeof is object and that are not null. Run it on [{}, [], null, 'x', 5] and print the count.
Write typeOfItems(list) that returns the shared typeof when every element has the same type and the word mixed when they do not. Test [1,2,3] and [1,'2'].
Write describeDeep(value) that reports array of number for [1, 2], date for a Date, null for null and the plain typeof for anything else. Print all four results.
Write describeCollection(value) that returns array of arrays of length 2 for [[1], [2]] and flat array of length 2 for [1, 2], and falls back to typeof for anything that is not an array.
Write sameDeepType(a, b) that is true when both values have the same typeof and are both arrays of the same length with matching element types. Test [1,2] against [1,2] and [1] against ['1'].
Write isText(value) that is true only for real string primitives, and run it over ['a', new String('a'), 1, ['a']]. Expected: true, false, false, false.
Parse the JSON string {"id":1,"tags":["a"],"ok":true} and print the typeof of every field as key:type pairs. Then print Array.isArray of the tags field next to its typeof.
answer:
JSON gives back plain objects, arrays and primitives, and an array lands on the object tag just like a null would.

code:
const payload = JSON.parse('{"id":1,"tags":["a"],"ok":true}');
const lines = Object.entries(payload).map(([key, value]) => key + ':' + typeof value);
console.log(lines.join(' ')); // id:number tags:object ok:boolean
console.log(Array.isArray(payload.tags), typeof payload.tags); // true object

output:
id:number tags:object ok:boolean
true object

question: Put JSON, Math and console.log in an array and print the typeof of each, then print the typeof of Math.max and of JSON.stringify.
answer:
JSON and Math are plain objects that hold functions as properties, so only the individual methods are functions. Check the tag of the value you are about to call.

code:
const builtins = [JSON, Math, console.log];
console.log(builtins.map((item) => typeof item).join(', ')); // object, object, function
console.log(typeof Math.max, typeof JSON.stringify); // function function
console.log(typeof JSON.parse('{}'), typeof JSON.stringify({})); // object string

output:
object, object, function
function function
object string

question: Declare a class Checkout with a total of 0 on the instance, create one, and print its typeof, the typeof of the class itself, and whether the instance is an instance of the class.

Write groupCount(values) that returns an object with the keys primitive and object counting how many values fall in each group, treating functions as objects. Run it on [1, 'a', {}, null, () => 1] and check where null lands.
Create the values 0xff, 0b101, 0o17, 1e3 and 1_000, print their typeof values joined by commas and the values themselves, then print whether 0o17 equals 15 and 1_000 equals 1000.
answer:
Every literal form is stored as a plain number, so the printed values prove the source notation does not survive into the type tag.

code:
const values = [0xff, 0b101, 0o17, 1e3, 1_000];
const tags = values.map((value) => typeof value);
console.log(tags.join(',')); // number,number,number,number,number
console.log(values.join(',')); // 255,5,15,1000,1000
console.log(0o17 === 15, 1_000 === 1000); // true true

output:
number,number,number,number,number
255,5,15,1000,1000
true true

question: Write typeOfNumber(value) that returns integer, decimal or not-a-number for 7, 7.5 and 'abc'. Print all three results.
Write describeFn(fn) that returns not a function for a string, has prototype for a normal function and arrow or method for an arrow function. Print all three results.
Declare const browser = 'chrome' and print the result of !typeof browser, of typeof browser === 'string' and of typeof browser.length.
answer:
typeof is a unary operator, so it binds tightly to the value and the result can be compared straight away.

code:
const browser = 'chrome';
console.log(!typeof browser); // false
console.log(typeof browser === 'string'); // true
console.log(typeof browser.length); // number

output:
false
true
number
